newsitem.title: USA: Jury selection in Simpson trial enters second week.
newsitem.headline: Jury selection in Simpson trial enters second week.

text.p: A woman who professed near-total ignorance of the most highly publicised murder case in U.S. history was accepted Tuesday as a prospective juror in the O. J. Simpson civil trial.

While others questioned during jury selection mostly expressed strong opinions about Simpson's guilt or innocence, Juror 39 -- a black woman in her 30s --left courtroom observers scratching their heads when she said she knew almost nothing about the case.

Simpson's criminal trial -- which ended last Oct. 3 with his acquittal in the murders of his former wife and one of her friends -- was broadcast live on national television, and millions followed every twist and turn of the sensational courtroom drama.

The former football star now faces wrongful-death civil suits brought by the families of victims Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman. Jury selection entered its fourth day Tuesday and was expected to last at least two to three weeks more.

Simpson seemed in high spirits as he looked on, occasionally whispering to his attorneys or rolling his eyes at a prospective juror's comments. During a break, he turned to his bodyguard and said jokingly: "You got 12 lawyers working for a defendant who is flat broke. That's a phenomenal thing."

Simpson, whose personal fortune was once estimated at $10 million, spent millions on his criminal defence, and the legal fees are now mounting for his civil trial. He faces no threat of jail time in his second trial but could be forced to pay heavy damages if he loses the case.

Tuesday's session opened with Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki scolding Goldman family attorney Daniel Petrocelli for failing to agree to dismiss automatically prospective jurors who say on their questionnaires that nothing could make them change their opinions on the case.

Attorneys for both sides huddled, and Petrocelli agreed to the immediate expulsion of 10 people from the jury pool of When the questioning of potential jurors got under way, opinions divided up mainly along racial lines, with whites tending to believe Simpson committed the murders and blacks more convinced of his innocence. Six of the first eight panellists who entered the courtroom were dismissed.

But Juror 39 was kept in the pool after telling attorneys she changed the channel when news reports about last year's trial came on television, tuned out co-workers who talked about the case and had no opinion about Simpson's guilt or innocence.
"I'm not really sure of what went on," she said. "I didn't have time. I work, and I have two kids."

Stan Goldman, a Loyola University law professor, said attorneys in the case "should take such statements with a grain of salt. You never know when someone wants to get on the trial because they have a hidden agenda," he said.
A black man in his 30s said he believed police had tampered with blood evidence in the case -- a major thrust of Simpson's defence in his criminal trial. He was dismissed.
A white man in his 40s and a white woman in her 50s both said they thought Simpson was "definitely guilty" of the murders. They were removed from the panel.
A black woman in her 50s said Simpson "didn't seem to have a motive" for the crime. She was dismissed.

Those who survive the latest phase of jury selection -- designed to weed out people prejudiced by publicity -- will move on to the the next, in which they will be questioned about race, domestic violence and other issues.
From that pool will come the 12 regular jurors who will decide the case plus eight alternates.
